phased-array-001.question: Which statement about the radiation pattern of an array antenna made of identical elements at equal spacing is correct? Ignore mutual coupling between the elements.
choices: It is the single-element pattern multiplied by the array factor (a factor set only by the element positions and the feed amplitudes and phases)
It is the radiation pattern of a single element plus the array factor, and as elements are added, the influence of the element's own directivity fades away
Whatever element is used, it is set by the array factor alone, and the single-element pattern affects neither the main-beam direction nor the sidelobes
phased-array-001.explanation: When every element radiates with the same shape and only the positions and the feed amplitudes and phases differ, the far field separates into "element pattern × array factor" (the principle of pattern multiplication). The array factor AF(θ) = Σ aₙ exp(jn(kd sinθ + β)) depends only on the element spacing d, the amplitudes aₙ and the phase difference β between neighbors, so the array part is calculated the same way whatever element is used. Because it is a product, not a sum, the influence of the element pattern does not disappear as elements are added, and the array cannot radiate in a direction where the element pattern is zero, even if the beam is steered there. The pattern is set by the array factor alone only in the ideal case of isotropic elements.

phased-array-002.question: In a linear array with element spacing d = λ/2, you want to steer the beam 30° from broadside (the direction normal to the array). What progressive phase shift must be applied between adjacent elements? Take the phase difference as Δφ = 2πd sinθ/λ.
phased-array-002.explanation: Δφ = 360° × (d/λ) × sinθ = 360° × 0.5 × 0.5 = 90°. In the 30° direction, the path of the wave from the neighboring element differs by d sinθ = λ/4, so if that much phase is supplied on the feed side, the waves from all elements line up in phase in that direction and reinforce one another. 180° is the value with the sinθ factor forgotten; it is the phase difference that points the beam to θ = 90° (along the axis of the array). 45° is the value calculated with an element spacing of λ/4. With zero phase difference, the beam points to broadside. Reversing the sign of the phase difference points it to −30° on the other side.

phased-array-003.question: Which statement about grating lobes of an array antenna is correct?
choices: Coupling between neighboring elements makes them appear more easily the narrower the spacing, so elements should be placed as far apart as possible, at least a wavelength
Adding elements makes the waves cancel in every direction except the main beam, so grating lobes can be eliminated regardless of element spacing
If the element spacing is larger than a wavelength, lobes as strong as the main beam appear in other directions even when the beam points to broadside
phased-array-003.explanation: Grating lobes appear because, in directions other than the main beam, the phase shift between neighboring elements can be exactly an integer multiple of 360°, so the waves from all elements reinforce one another as strongly as in the main beam. Their directions are given by sinθg = sinθ0 ± mλ/d, so even for a broadside beam (θ0 = 0), d > λ gives |sinθg| = λ/d < 1, a real direction. Scanning makes the condition stricter, requiring d < λ/(1 + |sinθ0|). Wider spacing makes them more likely, so the choice saying they appear more easily with narrower spacing has it backward. Adding elements only makes each lobe narrower; it does not change the direction or strength of the grating lobes.

phased-array-004.question: In a phased array used at 10 GHz, you want no grating lobes to appear even when the beam is scanned up to ±60° from broadside. Which is closest to the upper limit of the element spacing? Use the condition d < λ/(1 + |sinθ|), take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s and sin 60° ≈ 0.866.
choices: About 16 mm
15 mm
30 mm
phased-array-004.explanation: λ = c/f = 30 mm, so d < 30/(1 + 0.866) ≈ 16.1 mm. The larger the scan angle, the larger the denominator and the narrower the allowed spacing. 30 mm (one wavelength) is the condition d < λ for no scanning (θ = 0); when the beam is scanned to 60°, a grating lobe enters visible space. 15 mm (λ/2) is a commonly used conservative value at which no grating lobe appears even when scanning to ±90°, but it is not the upper limit for scanning up to ±60°. In practice, the spacing is made slightly narrower than the limit so that the skirt of the grating lobe does not enter visible space.

phased-array-005.question: On receive, an array antenna combines the outputs of 64 elements in phase. If the noise of each element is uncorrelated with the others and equal in power, which is closest to the improvement in S/N after combining compared with a single element (the array gain)?
choices: About 9 dB
About 36 dB
About 18 dB
phased-array-005.explanation: When aligned in phase, the signals add as voltages, so the combined signal power is N² times larger. Uncorrelated noise, on the other hand, adds as power and grows only N times. The S/N therefore improves by N²/N = N = 64 times, or 10 log₁₀ 64 ≈ 18 dB. About 36 dB looks only at the signal power growing N² times and forgets the increase in noise (20 log₁₀ 64). About 9 dB takes the improvement as √N. When the noise is correlated between elements (for example, interference arriving from one direction), this improvement is not obtained.

phased-array-006.question: In a transmitting phased array, the number of elements is doubled while the output of each element's amplifier and the gain of each element stay the same. By roughly how much does the EIRP in the broadside direction increase? Assume the same element spacing and ignore losses.
choices: About 3 dB
About 6 dB
About 12 dB
phased-array-006.explanation: Doubling the number of elements doubles the total transmit power combined in space (+3 dB), and at the same time doubles the aperture, which doubles the array gain (+3 dB). EIRP is the product of transmit power and gain, so it rises by about 6 dB in total, and EIRP is proportional to the square of the number of elements. About 3 dB counts only one of the two increases, power or gain. About 12 dB wrongly takes EIRP as proportional to the fourth power of the number of elements. A strength of the phased array is that even small amplifiers, lined up in numbers, give a large EIRP.

phased-array-007.question: For a uniform linear array (all elements with equal amplitude) with λ/2 spacing pointed at broadside, how do the half-power beamwidth and directivity of the main beam change when the number of elements is increased from 16 to 32?
choices: The half-power beamwidth becomes about 1/2, and the directivity rises by about 3 dB
The half-power beamwidth becomes about 1/4, and the directivity rises by about 6 dB
The half-power beamwidth does not change; only the sidelobes become lower as elements are added
phased-array-007.explanation: The half-power beamwidth of a uniform linear array at broadside is about 0.886λ/(Nd) rad, inversely proportional to the aperture length Nd. With d = λ/2, it is about 6.3° for N = 16 and about 3.2° for N = 32, roughly half. In a linear array, the beam narrows only in the plane along which the elements are lined up, so the directivity is proportional to N and doubles (about 3 dB). 1/4 and 6 dB confuse this with a planar array doubled in both directions (four times the elements). With uniform amplitude, the first sidelobe stays at about −13 dB regardless of the number of elements, and adding elements does not lower it.

phased-array-008.question: Which is correct about a planar phased array when its beam is steered to 60° from broadside? Ignore the effect of the element pattern and consider only the foreshortening of the aperture seen at an oblique angle.
choices: The aperture itself does not move and only the element phases change, so both the beamwidth and gain stay exactly the same as at broadside
Seen from an oblique direction the elements look more closely packed, so the beamwidth in the scan plane narrows to about 1/2 and the gain rises by about 3 dB
The apparent aperture shrinks by cos 60° = 0.5, so the beamwidth in the scan plane roughly doubles and the gain falls by about 3 dB
phased-array-008.explanation: Seen from the scan direction, the aperture is projected obliquely and appears shrunk to L cosθ. The beamwidth is inversely proportional to the apparent aperture, so at 60° it widens by about 1/cos 60° = 2 times, and the gain (effective aperture) falls by a factor of cosθ = 0.5, or about 3 dB (scan loss). The beamwidth in the plane orthogonal to the scan hardly changes. Changing the phases electronically does not move the aperture itself, so the beamwidth and gain do not stay the same as at broadside, let alone become sharper. In practice the element pattern also falls off at oblique angles, so the loss is usually even larger. For this reason the scan range of one array face is limited to about ±60°, and several faces pointing in different directions are combined to cover all directions.

phased-array-009.question: For a digital phase shifter that switches its phase shift in binary bits, what is the smallest phase step of a 6-bit device?
phased-array-009.explanation: An n-bit phase shifter divides 360° into 2ⁿ steps, so a 6-bit device has steps of 360°/64 = 5.625°. 60° wrongly divides 360° by the number of bits, 6. 11.25° is the step of a 5-bit (32-step) device. Coarse steps produce errors from rounding the phase needed at each element (quantization errors), which lead to beam-pointing errors, higher sidelobes and lower gain. When the rounding errors of the elements line up periodically, unwanted lobes called quantization lobes can also appear.

phased-array-010.question: Using phase shifters (which give a constant phase regardless of frequency), the phase of each element is set so that the beam points 30° from broadside at 10 GHz. If a 10.5 GHz signal is transmitted without changing the settings, which is closest to the beam direction?
choices: About 28.4°
About 31.7°
phased-array-010.explanation: The phase difference between neighboring elements, Δφ = 2πd sinθ/λ, is fixed, so the beam direction is set so that sinθ/λ stays constant. From sinθ = (f0/f) sinθ0 = (10/10.5) × 0.5 ≈ 0.476, θ ≈ 28.4°. As the frequency rises, the wavelength gets shorter and the path difference d sinθ that matches the same phase difference becomes smaller, so the beam moves toward broadside. About 31.7° applies the frequency ratio the wrong way round. The beam would stay at 30° with true time delay, which applies a time delay rather than a phase. This change of beam direction with frequency is called beam squint; with a wideband signal, the gain toward the target falls at the edges of the band.

phased-array-011.question: What is the main reason for using true-time-delay (TTD) elements instead of phase shifters in a phased array that handles wideband signals?
choices: Time-delay elements only switch line lengths and contain no active devices, so they have lower loss than phase shifters and zero insertion loss at every frequency
With time delay the element waves line up in only one direction, so grating lobes do not appear regardless of element spacing
Giving each element a time delay equal to the path difference d sinθ/c makes the waves line up in the same direction at every frequency, so beam squint does not occur
phased-array-011.explanation: The delay from the path difference, d sinθ/c, is a fixed time regardless of frequency. A phase shifter supplies a matching phase at only one frequency, so at other frequencies the beam direction shifts. If a time delay is applied instead, the required phase automatically scales in proportion to frequency, and the beam points in the same direction across the whole band. For example, with d = 15 mm and 30°, the delay difference between neighboring elements is 0.015 × 0.5/(3×10⁸) = 25 ps. Long delay lines, however, are large and lossy, so the insertion loss is not 0. The grating-lobe condition is set by element spacing and frequency and is not changed by how the delay is applied. In practice, configurations that put time delay only at the subarray level are also widely used.

phased-array-012.question: Which is a correct characteristic of analog beamforming (a scheme in which RF phase shifters adjust the phase of each element before combining, and the rest is handled by a single transceiver chain with an ADC and DAC)?
choices: Each element has its own ADC, and the weights can be reapplied digitally even after combining, so any number of beams in different directions can be formed at the same time
Only a single transceiver chain is needed, which keeps power consumption and cost down, but only one beam can be formed at a time, and its direction is switched over time
Signals are combined directly at RF, so neither phase shifters nor time delays are needed and beam squint cannot occur in principle, even for wideband signals
phased-array-012.explanation: In the analog scheme, a phase is applied to each element's signal at RF before combining, so only one transceiver chain (mixer, ADC and DAC and so on) follows, keeping power consumption and parts down even with many elements. In exchange, the combined signal corresponds to a beam in one direction, so only one beam can be handled at a time, and other directions are covered in turn by switching the beam over time. For this reason, the beam search for the direction of the other station takes time. Having an ADC for each element is digital beamforming. And since phase shifters apply the phase, beam squint occurs with wideband signals.

phased-array-013.question: Which is a correct characteristic of digital beamforming (a scheme in which each element has its own transceiver chain with an ADC and DAC, and weights are applied and combined by signal processing)?
choices: Applying different weights to the same received data forms several beams at once and can point nulls at interference, but per-element circuits make power consumption and data volume large
Signal processing removes the need for phase shifters, so it uses fewer circuits than analog beamforming and is the scheme with the lowest power consumption
Because the combining is digital, grating lobes do not appear even when the element spacing is made wider than in analog beamforming, at a wavelength or more
phased-array-013.explanation: In the digital scheme, each element's signal is digitized as it is, so it can be combined any number of times with different weights, making it easy to form several beams at once or to point a zero of gain (a null) toward incoming interference. Per-element time delays can also be applied in signal processing. On the other hand, a mixer and ADC/DAC are needed for every element, so power consumption, heat and data transfer grow, which becomes a heavy burden at millimeter waves where there may be hundreds of elements. It uses more circuits than the analog scheme, so the choice claiming fewer circuits and the lowest power consumption has it backward. Grating lobes are set by how coarsely the elements sample space, so digital combining does not change the condition d < λ/(1 + |sinθ|).

phased-array-014.question: A base station uses hybrid beamforming with 64 elements and 4 RF chains (transceiver circuits with ADC and DAC). Each RF chain drives many elements through analog phase shifters, and the digital stage processes the signals of the 4 chains. What is the upper limit on the number of independent data streams that can be sent at the same time? Assume the other end (such as the number of terminal antennas) is not the limiting factor.
phased-array-014.explanation: In the hybrid scheme, analog phase shifters combine many elements to form a beam, and the outputs are processed digitally for each RF chain. The number of signals that can be handled independently in the digital domain equals the number of RF chains, so the upper limit on simultaneous streams (or on beams pointed at different users at the same time) is 4. 64 is the number of elements; a digital scheme with an RF chain for every element could handle up to that many, as far as conditions at the other end allow. 16 is the number of elements divided by the number of RF chains, the elements per chain. The idea of the hybrid scheme is to secure beam sharpness and array gain with many elements while saving power by reducing the number of RF chains.

phased-array-015.question: The first sidelobe of a linear array with uniform amplitude is about 13 dB below the main beam. Which change is correct when an amplitude taper (a Taylor distribution, for example) that makes the amplitude smaller toward the edge elements is applied?
choices: The discontinuity at the edges disappears, so the sidelobes and the main-beam width both become smaller, and the gain also rises
The sidelobes fall, but the main beam widens and the gain falls slightly
The sidelobes stay at about −13 dB; only the grating lobes disappear
phased-array-015.explanation: A uniform amplitude distribution gives the narrowest beam and the highest gain for a given aperture size, but because the amplitude stops abruptly at the edges of the aperture, the first sidelobe is fairly high, at about −13 dB. Lowering the amplitude gradually toward the edges can bring the sidelobes down to about −30 dB, but the effective aperture shrinks because the edge elements do not fully contribute, so the main beam widens and the gain falls below the uniform case (taper loss). Sidelobes, beamwidth and gain cannot all be improved at once, so the choice claiming smaller sidelobes, a narrower beam and higher gain all together is wrong. Grating lobes are set by element spacing and are not removed by the amplitude distribution.
